doc.title: Danny Barker Interview (Louis Armstrong memorial broadcast), 1971-07-09

title: Singers as stylists: Cab Calloway, Fats Waller and Armstrong's trumpet power
summary: Barker and the host discuss singers as individual stylists, Cab Calloway's Jewish-flavored material, and why Armstrong moved from cornet to trumpet, with his barrel chest and power.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Growl, plunger and derby: the trumpet mute tradition

blocks.x: The music is considered singers. Oh, I see. But then you become a stylist. I see what you're saying. See, with Larry coming on, you become an individual stylist. So people say, well, he always sings cute. See, like, whole Carmichael, people will buy his records. He's got a little thing like something about China, a nice little record. Well, you like it. Yeah, he was really reciting to his music, really. He's not a guy, but he's a stylist. I see what you're saying. You've seen Fats Waller come on, doing his humor. And that was Cab Calloway, almost a perfect imitation of Lewis Scott singing. Right. Heideideho thing, he put the Jewish thing in there from the Jewish hymnal, you know. Yes. You know, you're the first person that ever, I've mentioned that in gospel. Ailey Ailey is the background of so much that we use. And I'm glad to hear you recognize that. But I didn't realize Cab Calloway. That's why the Jewish people identified with Cab, because, I mean, he was like a boy that's one of the rabbis, see? That's right. You're right. You're right. The fact that he did with Jewish people, because they had done those. Yes, and he would say, oy, oy, oy, so very, yes, yes. Much of them thought. Yeah, he'd done all them kind of tunes, Jewish tunes with Jewish humor in them, see? Oh, no. Arthur Zoya, the Taylor man. Yes, yes, that's Yiddish. Well, yes, well, he had this thing, see? Well, he got the publishers, they saw the potential with him. Well, then you... But, Lillard, you just put Lillard on the side. It's like you take Duke Allen thing, you put him on the side. I mean, that's something special. Then you take a drive and swing band, you put Basie on the side. I mean, that's other bands, you know, but leave them bands with me to do. In other words, they reached a point in this whole development of American music, they reached a point where they have made themselves, and all you can do is go in and say, well, I'm not... Well, the time you start playing something that them people do, they say, oh, I'm taking something from Duke. He's doing Duke Elton, or he's doing Mace. I see, yes, yes. Uh-huh. He's doing Lewis. Yeah. Right away, you know. Uh-huh. And this... Now, Louis played the trumpet and the cornet. Can you explain? A lot of persons said he gave up... He gave up the... The cornet. He gave up one for the other. Was there any real reason for that, or was that... Was that something that musicians would ordinarily do, or was that... What was behind that? Well, no. With the coming of Lewis's cornets, and with the coming of Lewis and his power and his drive and his force, and the pinnacle of notes he hit with such brilliancy, the horn makers began to make trumpets of different dimensions of the pipe. I see. So you'd get a higher brilliancy. I see. They used different mouth to... The guys wanted... They used to call them T-shooters. A little mouthpiece with small holes... Yes, yes. ...so you could scream up the nose. Yes. Well, Lewis done it naturally. If you ever noticed Lewis's body, if you saw him in the dressing room, he has a barrel chest. He has terrific strong lips and this power of pressure from the lips. And what he's doing, he had the facility with his fingers, and his soul and his fill. When he came out, there's no horn sound like his horn. I've seen Lewis at concerts. There'd be five or six trumpet players and all kinds of musicians tuning up, and Lewis will come in, take his horn out of the case, and hit three or four notes. You have all these... You hear all these horns, blubber by this... And you hear Lewis say... I remember that. ...you hear Oakland singing.... ...you hear Oakland singing.... ...you hear Oakland singing....
